explain.say: At Christmas 1831 in Jamaica, Sam Sharpe, an enslaved Baptist preacher, called a peaceful strike. It grew into a huge rising of perhaps 60,000 people, the Baptist War. It was crushed, and Sharpe was hanged in 1832. Yet within two years Britain's Parliament voted to end slavery in most of its colonies. Look at the timeline of abolitions.

explain.say: Why did slavery end? See the reasons. First, enslaved people resisted, from Haiti to Jamaica. Then mass campaigns: Olaudah Equiano's life story, petitions with huge numbers of signatures, and women organising boycotts of slave-grown sugar. Quakers and evangelicals called slavery a sin. Which cause do older textbooks often forget?

draw.answer: Many forces together, starting with the enslaved.

explain.say: Now the sizes, all approximate. Abolition in British colonies, from 1834, affected about 800,000 people; the United States freed about 4 million in 1865; Brazil about 700,000 in 1888. Britain paid 20 million pounds in compensation, to the slave owners, not the enslaved, who had to work years more as so-called apprentices. How does that strike you?

draw.text: Loans raised for that compensation were finally repaid in 2015.

explain.say: The map shows the long road. France ended slavery again in 1848. In the United States the Civil War led to the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. Brazil was the last country in the Americas: on 13 May 1888 the Golden Law, signed by Princess Isabel, freed everyone still enslaved. Why do you think Brazil held on so long?

Now the great debate. Eric Williams, later Trinidad's first prime minister, argued in 1944 that abolition came when slavery stopped paying. Seymour Drescher replied that it was still profitable, so Britain gave up money for moral reasons. Thoughtful work. Exam tip: add the enslaved people's own actions to both arguments.

faq.a: Through a mix of resistance by enslaved people, mass campaigns of petitions and boycotts, religious and Enlightenment arguments, economic and political change, and in the United States a civil war. Historians weigh these causes differently.
asks: What ended slavery in the British Empire?

faq.q: Did Britain end slavery for economic reasons?
faq.a: Eric Williams argued in Capitalism and Slavery, 1944, that slavery was declining in value and industrial interests wanted free trade. Seymour Drescher argued in Econocide, 1977, that slavery was still profitable, so abolition cost Britain money and was driven by public moral pressure.

faq.q: What did the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 do?
faq.a: It ended slavery in most British colonies from 1 August 1834, but forced freed people into unpaid apprenticeship until 1838 and paid 20 million pounds in compensation to slave owners. The enslaved received nothing.
asks: Who was compensated when slavery ended?

faq.a: A rising of perhaps 60,000 enslaved people in Jamaica at Christmas 1831, led by the Baptist deacon Sam Sharpe. It was suppressed with great brutality, but it pushed Parliament towards abolition.
On 13 May 1888, through the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law, signed by Princess Isabel. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

facts: Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807.
The Slavery Abolition Act came into force on 1 August 1834.
Brazil abolished slavery on 13 May 1888 with the Lei Áurea.
